title: Wounds, Rifts, and Wars
hook: Megan touches the dented guardrail and feels an old lockout trying to vote on a new safety defect.
counterintuition: A wound can stay real while the story built around it becomes dangerous. Group innocence turns pain into permission when no one may name the next blow.
tryThisNow: For one group you belong to, write two true sentences: what was done to us, and what that history gives us no permission to do now.
keyTakeaway: Protect the truth of a group wound without letting shared innocence become moral permission for retaliation.

breakdown.fastRead:
"They have never cared about our safety," someone says as the dented guard lies across the bargaining-room credenza. Megan remembers the lockout too. The wound is real.

Then she separates it from the current guardrail defect before the committee vote. The lockout belongs in the room, but it cannot cast the only ballot.

Groups defend themselves by turning injury into identity. Each side calls its own blow context and the other side’s blow character. From there, payback starts to feel like memory doing its duty.
breakdown.deepRead:
The foam-board zoning map leans on a scratched folding table while Olivier listens to long-time residents and new apartment owners accuse each other of erasing the block. The last project hurt people. The current costs are not identical.

Olivier can see us-versus-them escalation begin when each group preserves its own innocence and reads the other side as the real aggressor. Our pressure was forced. Their pressure reveals who they are. Our hard line is defense. Their hard line is menace. Once that split becomes collective memory, every new decision arrives already morally sorted.

Pain is not the problem. Permission is.

Marit sees a group remember a real injury and still use that injury inside a self-renewing conflict story. Loyalty makes this harder to interrupt. Naming your own side's aggression can feel like betrayal of the wounded. Questioning the grievance can sound like forgetting. That is why the story polices its own members before it ever faces the other side.

The limit matters. This is not a plea to flatten all harms or call every side equally guilty. Some wounds are larger, older, and more consequential. The discipline is to keep the wound true while refusing to let it authorize whatever comes next.
breakdown.fullRead:
Which faction will call the moderation log betrayal, and which will call it overdue order? Marit can predict both answers before she opens the laptop. The banned contributor broke a rule. The moderators also skipped a promised warning. Each faction wants one fact and not the other.

That is how grievance becomes identity. The record stops being a record and becomes a loyalty test. To mention the rule breach is to betray one side. To mention the process miss is to excuse chaos for the other. Two true facts cannot sit together because each group has made innocence into property.

A wound can remain true and still become the passport a group uses to cross into retaliation.

The phrase injury as identity names a dangerous transformation. At first, a group remembers what happened so it will not be harmed again. Later, remembering becomes part of what proves membership. Certain details become sacred. Certain admissions become taboo. Certain questions mark you as someone who has forgotten who the victims are supposed to be.

Sam sees the local version during the school merger. The faded mascot patch carries an old closure fight. Enrollment numbers carry the current need. If either town gets to claim pure victimhood, bus routes and mascot choices will become symbols in a conflict that no longer has to answer to children sitting on buses. The old wound matters. It cannot be allowed to replace the current map.

A fair objection belongs here: groups often need shared memory to survive. Forgetting harm can be another form of harm. The answer is not amnesia. The answer is moral bookkeeping with two columns. What was done to us. What we have done or are tempted to do under that banner. A group that cannot write the second column has turned memory into permission.

Javier faces that tension in the museum label draft. The acquisition record must be named. The harmed group should not be asked to soften the wound for institutional comfort. Yet the institution also has to name its choice plainly rather than hiding behind abstract history. The label must hold truth without using truth as an excuse for delay, defensiveness, or retaliation in another form.

Adaeze brings the same move to the refugee association board. Older arrivals endured real hardship. Newly arrived families still need aid. She writes two true sentences: we survived being denied help, and that history gives us no right to deny newcomers a fair allocation now. The first sentence preserves identity. The second prevents identity from becoming gatekeeping.

Retaliation loops feed on selective memory. One side's counterblow becomes fresh proof for the other side. The next hardening then feels necessary, which creates more proof in return. No participant has to feel cruel. Each side only has to feel innocent enough.

The exit begins before reconciliation. It begins when a group can name its wound and its next temptation in the same breath.

examples.title: Megan Separates the Guardrail Vote

planSpec.domain: a union-management safety committee after a bruising lockout
planSpec.audience: workplace groups carrying institutional memory into negotiations
planSpec.stakes: a new guardrail dispute may become proof that the other side never changes
planSpec.requiredBeat: Megan separates the lockout wound from the current guardrail defect before the committee votes to retaliate procedurally

examples.scenario: At 2:40 PM in the union safety committee room, Megan hears, "They never cared about safety," while the dented guard lies across the bargaining-room credenza. The lockout wound is real, and the current defect still needs a vote. Before the committee retaliates procedurally, she must decide how to name the lockout wound and the guardrail evidence as separate facts.
examples.whatToDo: Name the lockout as real history, then return to the current guardrail defect and the repair vote. Keep memory from casting the whole ballot.
examples.whyItMatters: The old injury explains distrust, but it can also make every defect proof that the other side never changes. Separation protects the safety decision.

examples.title: Olivier Maps Loss and Cost

planSpec.domain: a neighborhood redevelopment forum between long-time residents and new apartment owners
planSpec.audience: civic groups whose identity is built around being harmed or ignored
planSpec.stakes: a zoning meeting becomes a ritual of accusation rather than a decision about one block
planSpec.requiredBeat: Olivier maps who lost what in the last project and who would bear costs now, preventing either side from using one wound as the whole map

examples.scenario: A foam-board zoning map leans on a scratched folding table in the school gym. Olivier draws one circle around what long-time residents lost in the last project and another around who pays the current cost. The speakers’ line is growing. Before the vote, he has to choose a two-map record over one wound carrying the whole block.
examples.whatToDo: Map past loss and current cost separately before public comment resumes. Make each side specify which harm belongs to which decision.
examples.whyItMatters: When one wound becomes the whole map, every current choice turns into accusation. Separate maps keep history true and decisions visible.

examples.title: Marit Posts Both Facts

planSpec.domain: an online fan community split after moderators banned a popular contributor
planSpec.audience: community leaders watching grievance turn into identity badges
planSpec.stakes: every moderation decision becomes evidence of betrayal or chaos
planSpec.requiredBeat: Marit predicts both factions' interpretation of the same moderation log, then posts the rule breach and the process miss together

examples.scenario: Which fact will each faction reject first? Marit watches the moderation queue glow on her laptop in the spare room. She predicts one side will call the ban betrayal and the other will call it overdue order. Before she posts, she must decide whether to publish both the rule breach and the skipped warning, forcing the community to face a whole log over identity badges.
examples.whatToDo: Post the rule breach and the process miss in the same update. Refuse to let either faction keep only the fact that preserves innocence.
examples.whyItMatters: A split community turns records into loyalty tests. Holding both facts interrupts the grievance story before it hardens into identity.

examples.title: Sam Reads Both Records

planSpec.domain: a regional school merger committee balancing two towns with a long rivalry
planSpec.audience: public officials handling inherited group memory
planSpec.stakes: bus routes and mascot choices become carriers for older humiliation
planSpec.requiredBeat: Sam reads the old closure minutes and the current enrollment numbers in the same meeting before letting either town claim pure victimhood

examples.scenario: At 6:05 PM, Sam tapes a faded mascot patch beside the enrollment chart. The old closure minutes are on the table, and both towns are ready to claim pure victimhood. Before bus routes and mascot choices become symbols, Sam must decide to read the old injury and the current numbers in the same meeting.
examples.whatToDo: Read the closure minutes and enrollment numbers together. Let neither town use old humiliation to erase present student needs.
examples.whyItMatters: Inherited memory can turn logistics into identity war. Two records keep the merger from being decided by a single innocence story.

examples.title: Javier Holds the Label Steady

planSpec.domain: a museum repatriation working group after a disputed exhibit label
planSpec.audience: institutions and community representatives balancing truth, injury, and defensiveness
planSpec.stakes: one side may treat any admission as betrayal while the other treats any delay as denial
planSpec.requiredBeat: It takes Javier two drafts to write a label that names the institution's acquisition choice without asking the harmed group to soften the wound

examples.scenario: At 11:20 AM in the museum gallery, Javier stands under the track lighting and stops protecting the institution. The blank exhibit label sits beside the acquisition record. Before community review ends, he has to choose whether the label names the institution’s acquisition choice without asking the harmed group to soften the wound.
examples.whatToDo: Name the acquisition choice plainly and keep the wound intact. Do not trade truth for institutional comfort or delay.
examples.whyItMatters: Admission can feel like betrayal inside the institution. Clear wording keeps defensiveness from turning injury into another contest over innocence.

examples.title: Adaeze Writes Two Sentences

planSpec.domain: a refugee association board split between older arrivals and newly arrived families
planSpec.audience: community groups where past survival can become current gatekeeping
planSpec.stakes: aid allocation becomes a moral contest over who suffered correctly
planSpec.requiredBeat: You watch Adaeze write two true sentences: what the older group endured, and what that history does not entitle them to deny newcomers

examples.scenario: At 3:30 PM in the aid-board office, you watch translated intake forms sit under a chipped ceramic paperweight while Adaeze writes two sentences for the board. The older arrivals were denied help for years. That history gives us no right to deny new families a fair aid review. Before allocation starts, the board has to choose memory as guidance or memory as gatekeeping.
examples.whatToDo: Write both sentences into the agenda before aid allocation. Honor the older wound while blocking it from becoming permission to exclude.
examples.whyItMatters: Survival history can become a badge that polices newcomers. The second sentence keeps identity from becoming a weapon.

questions.prompt: A safety committee treats every new management error as proof that the lockout wound never ended. What should it separate first?
choices: The current defect from any need to act.
The union’s feelings from all safety evidence.
The real lockout history from the current defect and repair vote.
questions.explanation: The lockout matters, but it should not decide every current fact. Separation protects both memory and repair.

questions.prompt: At a packed redevelopment forum in the school gym, residents use the last project’s harm to block any discussion of current rent and traffic costs. Which move best keeps old injury and present cost visible?
choices: Tell residents to move on from old losses.
Map past loss and present cost separately before the vote.
Let new owners decide because they were not involved.
questions.explanation: Separate maps preserve the old harm while making the current decision visible. Moving on or handing control away avoids the real tension.

questions.prompt: In an online community dispute, moderators have one fact that makes each faction look innocent and one fact that makes each faction look responsible. What should the moderator publish?
choices: Only the rule breach to restore order.
Only the process miss to show fairness.
The rule breach and the skipped warning together.
questions.explanation: Both facts interrupt factional innocence. A single favored fact feeds the grievance identity on one side.

questions.prompt: During a school merger meeting, two towns both claim pure victimhood while arguing over buses, mascots, and enrollment numbers. Which record pair best slows escalation?
choices: Old closure minutes and current enrollment numbers.
Mascot history and sports trophies.
Personal speeches from the loudest residents.
questions.explanation: The minutes honor inherited injury, and enrollment numbers show present needs. The other records may intensify identity claims.

questions.prompt: A museum label draft hides the institution’s acquisition choice because admission feels disloyal. What is the better move?
choices: Use abstract wording so both sides can accept it.
Delay the label until no one feels accused.
Name the acquisition choice without asking the harmed group to soften the wound.
questions.explanation: Clear wording accepts institutional responsibility. Delay and abstraction protect innocence while asking the wound to shrink.

questions.prompt: Older members of an association endured real exclusion and now want to restrict aid to newcomers. What sentence should be added?
choices: Our history proves we deserve all aid first.
What we endured gives us no permission to deny a fair review now.
Newcomers should not mention their needs yet.
questions.explanation: The sentence preserves the older wound and blocks it from becoming gatekeeping. The other choices turn history into permission.

questions.prompt: A union member worries that naming her side’s procedural retaliation will sound like betrayal of coworkers hurt in the lockout. Why does group loyalty make self-examination costly?
choices: Questioning the group’s innocence can feel like betrayal of the wounded.
Groups are unable to remember facts accurately.
Loyal members always prefer retaliation.
questions.explanation: Loyalty can police memory by treating admission as betrayal. That does not mean groups lack facts or always seek revenge.

questions.prompt: In a public conflict, each group says its own hard line is forced by context while the other side’s hard line reveals character. What pattern is operating?
choices: A completed repair process.
Neutral historical review.
Us-versus-them self-justification.
questions.explanation: Each side grants itself context and reads the other as essence. That asymmetry fuels escalation.

questions.prompt: A community leader wants to honor a real group wound during a policy vote without letting that wound license the next unfair action. Which practice is strongest?
choices: Write what was done to us and what it gives us no permission to do now.
Ban discussion of the wound during decisions.
Let the angriest members define the next action.
questions.explanation: Two true sentences preserve memory and constrain permission. Silence and anger-led action each keep the loop alive.

reviewCards.front: What happens when injury becomes identity?
reviewCards.back: The wound becomes central to who the group believes it is. That memory can preserve truth, but it can also license the next harm.

reviewCards.front: How does us-versus-them escalation distort judgment?
reviewCards.back: Each side treats its own aggression as context and the other side’s aggression as character. The same action receives different moral names.

reviewCards.front: What should a group write when it feels justified by harm?
reviewCards.back: Write two sentences: what was done to us, and what that history gives us no permission to do now.

reviewCards.front: Why is naming your own group’s aggression so hard?
reviewCards.back: Loyalty can make admission feel like betrayal. The story protects its members by policing what details can be said.

reviewCards.front: What is the difference between preserving pain and preserving grievance?
reviewCards.back: Preserving pain keeps truth in view. Preserving grievance turns truth into a standing permission slip for retaliation or exclusion.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice holding two group truths at once. The skill is to preserve the reality of injury while naming what the injury does not permit now. This interrupts retaliation before it can borrow moral authority from memory.

ifThenPlans.plan: If an old wound enters a current vote, then name the wound and the current evidence as separate items.
If one past project becomes the whole map, then draw past loss and present cost on separate records.
If factions each want only one fact posted, then publish the rule breach and the process miss together.
If survival history starts deciding who deserves help, then add the sentence that history gives no permission to exclude.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: For one group you belong to, write two true sentences: what was done to us, and what that history gives us no permission to do now.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: This week, notice one group story that makes your side purely innocent. Add one fact about your side’s conduct or temptation that the story usually leaves out.

memorableLines.text: The lockout belongs in the room, but it cannot cast the only ballot.
memorableLines.why: It captures the balance between honoring harm and blocking permission.
The punch line clarifies that the target is permission, not memory.

memorableLines.text: Two true facts cannot sit together because each group has made innocence into property.
memorableLines.why: It names the group-level mechanism in a memorable way.
